key_insight: The title argues that as AI makes criticism easier to generate at scale, peer review needs a threshold for which critiques require a response. The supplied abstract repeats the title and provides no substantive findings, so this summary is a title-based interpretation.
problem_solved: AI-assisted criticism could produce more objections than authors and reviewers can reasonably address, creating a need to distinguish substantive concerns from low-value critique.
method: Conceptual framing: examine the burden created by scalable AI-assisted criticism.
Proposed principle: establish an obligation threshold for critiques that warrant a response.
The supplied text does not specify threshold criteria, implementation details, or empirical evaluation.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this framing highlights the need to balance AI-enabled scrutiny with manageable review workloads. It suggests that generating more criticism should not automatically create more obligations for authors.
visual_elements: A funnel showing a large volume of AI-generated critiques filtered into actionable concerns.
A threshold line separating critiques requiring a response from those below the obligation threshold, with criteria marked as unspecified.
A balance scale contrasting critical scrutiny with author and reviewer workload.
A workflow diagram linking AI-assisted criticism, editorial triage, and author response.
paper_title: When AI-assisted criticism scales, peer review needs an obligation threshold
paper_authors: Yiteng Sun, Fan Li, Ching-Hung Lee, Chun-Hsien Chen
